disclaimer: JobCheck SA is a heuristic aid. It can miss scams and it can flag legitimate adverts. A score is not a guarantee that an advert is safe or fraudulent.
next_steps: Verify the employer on the CIPC company search before you share documents or money. Look up the registered name, not only a logo, a WhatsApp display name, or an email signature. The public search is on CIPC eServices.
Never pay a fee, deposit, starter-kit cost, or registration charge to be hired, interviewed, or placed on a learnership. A legitimate employer pays you.
Do not send your ID number, a copy of your ID, bank details, or a SARS tax number before you have verified the company and attended a real interview.

If you have already paid or shared banking details, contact your bank at once and report the matter to the South African Police Service (SAPS). Banking-related fraud can also be reported to SABRIC, the South African Banking Risk Information Centre.
Prefer the company's own careers address or a published switchboard. Treat WhatsApp-only, Telegram-only, and free-mail recruiters as unverified until you can tie them to a registered business.

rules.name: Upfront fees
rules.explanation: The ad asks you to pay to be hired. Training, admin, registration, uniform, medical, or starter-kit fees are a common South African job scam. A real employer does not charge you to start work.

rules.name: ID, bank, or SARS details
rules.explanation: The ad asks for an ID number, a copy of your ID, bank details, or a SARS tax number. Those details are abused for identity fraud and do not belong in an application before you have verified the employer and been interviewed.

rules.name: Package reshipping
rules.explanation: The ad asks you to receive parcels and send them on. That is the parcel-mule pattern: the goods are often stolen or bought with stolen cards, and the person who reships them can be left to answer for it.

rules.name: SETA learnership fee
rules.explanation: The ad asks you to pay to join a SETA learnership. Real SETA learnerships are funded and often pay the learner a stipend. A fee to enrol is a known scam.

rules.name: Crypto or forex trading
rules.explanation: The ad recruits you into crypto or forex trading. Fake trading jobs and funded-account schemes are a common way to take fees or collect identity documents.

rules.name: Unrealistic pay
rules.explanation: The pay on offer is far above a normal wage for the work described, such as thousands of rand a day, or a high salary paired with no experience. Inflated pay is a common lure. Daily rates for scarce professional locum work can also match, so read the rest of the ad.

rules.name: Guaranteed job
rules.explanation: The ad promises a job, income, or 100% placement. Legitimate employers interview people. They do not guarantee employment in the advert.

rules.name: WhatsApp or Telegram contact
rules.explanation: The ad uses WhatsApp or Telegram as a contact channel. Scam recruiters prefer those apps because a chat is harder to tie to a registered company than a switchboard or a company domain. A real employer that also publishes a WhatsApp line can match this rule.

rules.name: Vague company or no address
rules.explanation: The ad does not give you a traceable employer. A withheld company name, a confidential location, or no street address makes a CIPC search much harder.

missing.snippet: No registered company name or street address was found.

rules.name: Free email address
rules.explanation: The recruiter uses a free inbox such as Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook (including Hotmail and Live), or webmail. A company hiring under its own name usually writes from its own domain, which you can compare with the company website.

rules.name: Urgency and pressure
rules.explanation: The ad pushes you to act immediately, for example with limited spots or a same-day start. Pressure is used to stop you checking the employer. On its own this is a weak signal, because ordinary vacancies can also be urgent.
